Who Said It, and When?

The family's notes about Mom's support in one place: where each one is kept, who it came from, and how old it is.

Download PDF

Your brother says the neighbor is glad to keep driving. He heard it from Mom, who heard it in the driveway last spring. The neighbor's phone number is in Mom's address book and nowhere else.

This page doesn't ask you to judge any of it. It asks where each note or number is kept, who it came from, and how old it is.

What to collectWhere it's keptWho it came fromIts date
Any list or notes the family has already made about Mom's week
Anything a professional has written for Mom that she's chosen to share, such as a visit summary
Phone numbers for the people who help: the neighbor, family, friends
Mom's doctors and her pharmacy, with phone numbers
Emergency contacts
Her standing appointments, and where the appointment card or calendar lives
Her usual routine, if anyone has written it down
The list of regular bills someone handles for her, and who keeps it
Texts, emails or notes where someone offered to help or agreed to fill in
Any calendar or message group the family uses for Mom's week

Scroll sideways to see every column, or print this page to fill it in.

What the family has only been told

Some of what the family knows about Mom's support was never written anywhere. Give each one a line: what was said, who told you, who they heard it from, and roughly when. Don't decide here whether it still holds.

What was saidWho told youWho they heard it fromWhen
“The neighbor is glad to keep driving.”My brotherMom, who heard it from the neighborLast spring

Scroll sideways to see every column, or print this page to fill it in.

What's missing, and who will ask for it

Anything above with an empty line. Put a name next to each.

For example Nobody but Mom has the neighbor's phone number. I'll ask Mom for it on Sunday.

How to use it

  • Write the date on each item. If it has none, write “undated,” or your best guess with a question mark.
  • Don't rewrite or summarize anything here. Just say where it is.
  • Mom's papers and phone numbers are hers to share. Ask her before you collect them.
  • Keep this page where the family can find it, and bring it to the next conversation about Mom's week.

What this page doesn't do

It doesn't explain what any note or record means, and it doesn't say whether something the family was told still holds. If you read something you don't understand, that's a question for the person who wrote it.

Where this comes from

The rows for Mom's doctors and for emergency contacts follow what the CDC says a care plan should list. The rows for key contacts, standing appointments and her usual routine follow what the Family Caregiver Alliance suggests writing down for whoever fills in. The rest come from the Family Care Roadmap's working list for this step.
